beats.narration_text: The data is public. The Department of Labor publishes a disclosure file of Labor Condition Applications, the form an employer files before hiring someone on an H one B. Each row has the employer, the job title, the city, and the wage. As an international student, that's what I want to know. But it's one giant spreadsheet.

beats.narration_text: Here's how it will work. You ask a question. Claude writes S Q L, following a written contract: the columns, and the rules for what it may write. The query runs, and returns an answer. Then the part that matters. It's compared with an answer I worked out myself, and marked pass, or fail.

beats.narration_text: Tools like this already exist, so I tested one. On October twenty-fourth, I gave Chat G P T the record layout, and one question. It wrote a careful query, and listed fifteen assumptions, like only checking the first worksite on each filing. When I asked it to run the query, it reported forty. But that was its own query, checking itself, and nobody has independently checked that number. I haven't tested Vanna A I this way. Sponsor S Q L will check every answer against one I worked out by hand.
beats.new_visual_element: ChatGPT lane shows the real test: a query, '15 assumptions', 'first worksite only', no count. Vanna lane dashed: not tested. SponsorSQL lane: check + failure log.

beats.narration_text: What will it prove? Four things this course teaches. A prompt contract: the schema, and the rules. Verification: every answer checked against one I verified by hand. Evaluation: a failure rate on a fixed test set. And source grounding: every answer names its year, its file, and its query.

beats.narration_text: In, out, and first. In: the latest file, fiscal twenty twenty-six through June, loaded into Duck D B, without its personal contact columns. Out: it won't predict sponsorship, or give legal advice. An L C A filing isn't a job offer, or an approved visa, and the tool will say so. First: ten questions, a hand-checked answer key, and a pass-fail table you can rerun.

beats.narration_text: What could sink it? Messy names. One company can appear under slightly different spellings, and the file even has a separate field for trade names. So Claude's S Q L could look right, and still undercount. I'll write test questions around exactly these traps, log every mismatch, and if Claude keeps missing them, show the matching rows instead of one total.

beats.narration_text: Why this project? It's a mix of showing off, and learning. I already use S Q L, Python, pandas, and B I dashboards, from earlier academic and professional work. What's new is building an evaluation harness for S Q L an A I wrote, and reporting its failures honestly. And I'm an international student. This is my question too.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Here is a S Q L query, and the question it answers. Before I trust it, list three ways it could return a wrong count, and write one test for each. Try it on any query an A I wrote for you, and check whether those tests would really catch the mistakes it names.
